title: Anticoagulants: Warfarin vs Heparins vs DOACs

questions.stem: A patient has atrial fibrillation and a mechanical mitral valve. Which anticoagulant is best?
questions.explanation: D is correct: with a mechanical heart valve, warfarin is the choice. A, apixaban, and C, rivaroxaban, are direct oral anticoagulants, which are not used with mechanical valves. B, dabigatran, is also a direct oral anticoagulant and was even harmful in patients with mechanical valves.

questions.stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation and no heart valve problem starts warfarin. What is the usual international normalized ratio (INR) goal?

options.text: No INR goal; warfarin needs no blood tests

questions.explanation: A is correct: for most patients, like atrial fibrillation or a blood clot in a vein, the goal is 2 to 3. B is close to a normal, untreated value and gives too little protection. C is above the usual goal and raises bleeding risk. D is wrong because warfarin is followed with the INR blood test.

questions.stem: A patient stable on warfarin is started on a new drug. Which of these are expected to push the INR up? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A, C, D, and F are correct: sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, metronidazole, fluconazole, and amiodarone all push the INR up, raising bleeding risk. B, rifampin, and E, carbamazepine, pull the INR down, so the clot risk rises instead.

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin loves salads and asks whether to give up leafy greens. What is the best counseling?

options.text: Eat as many greens as possible to protect the liver
Keep vitamin K intake steady from week to week
Take a daily vitamin K supplement with each dose

questions.explanation: C is correct: keep vitamin K intake steady, not zero, so the INR stays stable. A is wrong because zero is not the goal; a sudden drop in greens can push the INR up. B, a big jump in greens, adds vitamin K and pulls the INR down. D adds vitamin K directly, which works against warfarin.

questions.stem: On day 7 of a heparin infusion, a patient's platelets have fallen by more than half. What is the best action?

options.text: Stop all heparin, including flushes, and start argatroban
Continue heparin because low platelets lower clot risk

questions.explanation: C is correct: this points to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, so stop all heparin, even flushes, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban. A keeps giving heparin, which keeps the immune reaction going. B is wrong because enoxaparin is also a heparin and must be stopped too. D is wrong because in this reaction low platelets actually raise the risk of clots.

questions.stem: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is suspected in a patient on a heparin infusion with heparin line flushes. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban

questions.explanation: A, C, and E are correct: stop all heparin, including the flushes, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban. B is wrong because even the small amount of heparin in flushes keeps the reaction going. D is wrong because enoxaparin is a heparin and must be stopped too.

questions.stem: A patient on enoxaparin has a creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. What change is needed?

options.text: No change; enoxaparin is not affected by the kidneys
Double the dose to make up for faster clearance

questions.explanation: D is correct: the enoxaparin dose is lowered when creatinine clearance is below 30, and 24 is below 30. A is wrong because enoxaparin builds up when the kidneys are weak. C is wrong because the INR follows warfarin, not enoxaparin. B is wrong because weak kidneys clear enoxaparin more slowly, not faster, so doubling raises bleeding risk.

questions.stem: Which lab test is used to adjust an IV unfractionated heparin infusion?

options.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time or a factor ten (anti-Xa) level
No routine lab test is needed

questions.explanation: A is correct: regular heparin given in the vein is checked with the activated partial thromboplastin time, or a factor ten blood level. B, the INR, follows warfarin. C, kidney function, guides direct oral anticoagulant and enoxaparin doses, not the heparin rate. D describes enoxaparin, not an IV heparin infusion.

questions.stem: Which anticoagulant and reversal pairings are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warfarin: vitamin K, plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for a serious bleed

questions.explanation: B, C, and E are correct: idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, vitamin K (plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for a serious bleed) reverses warfarin, and protamine reverses heparin. A is wrong because vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin. D is wrong because protamine is for heparin; for factor ten blockers like apixaban, most hospitals now use four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate by protocol.

questions.stem: A patient is starting apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Which monitoring guides the dose?
questions.explanation: B is correct: direct oral anticoagulants need no routine INR checks, but you always check kidney function to choose the dose. A, the INR, follows warfarin. C follows IV heparin. D, platelet watching, is for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia on heparin.
